questions.question: For a binary linear code with parity-check matrix H, which condition defines the codewords?
options: All codewords c satisfy H·c^T = 0 over GF(2)
All codewords c satisfy G·c^T = 0 over GF(2)
All codewords c are the rows of H by definition
All codewords c have Hamming weight exactly t
questions.explanation: A parity-check matrix defines the code as the kernel: codewords are precisely the binary vectors with zero syndrome H·c^T.

questions.question: In GF(2^m) implemented in a polynomial basis, what operation corresponds to field addition?
options: Bitwise XOR of the m coefficient bits (coefficient-wise mod-2 add)
Integer addition then reduce modulo 2^m (treat elements as integers)
Integer addition then reduce modulo an irreducible polynomial (as written)
Bitwise AND of the m coefficient bits (a bit trick, not a field add)
questions.explanation: In characteristic 2, coefficient-wise addition is mod 2, which is exactly XOR on the bit representation.

questions.question: Why must every support element L_i satisfy g(L_i) != 0 in the Goppa parity-check construction used here?
options: So that 1/g(L_i) exists and the matrix entries are defined
So that g(x) is monic and has leading coefficient 1
So that L_i values can be expanded into exactly m bits
So that the code’s block length n equals 2^m exactly
questions.explanation: The alternant/Goppa parity-check uses factors 1/g(L_i); if g(L_i)=0 then division is undefined and the construction breaks.

questions.question: If g(x) has degree t over GF(2^m) and the support has length n, what is the shape of the expanded binary parity-check matrix H_bin in this lesson?
options: (m·t) × n over GF(2)
t × (m·n) over GF(2)
t × n over GF(2^m)
m × (t·n) over GF(2^m)
questions.explanation: Each of the t field rows expands into m binary rows by coefficient expansion, giving m·t rows total and n columns.

questions.question: How does the lesson obtain a generator matrix for the toy code from H_bin?
options: Compute a basis of the nullspace of H_bin over GF(2)
Invert H_bin over GF(2) and read off the rows as generators
Multiply H_bin by a random permutation matrix until systematic
Use g(x) as the generator polynomial and shift it to form rows
questions.explanation: A generator matrix can be taken as any basis of the kernel of H_bin; those basis vectors are valid codewords.

questions.question: What does the syndrome s = H_bin·r^T tell you about a received binary word r?
options: s = 0 means r is a codeword; s != 0 means r violates checks
s = 0 means r has no bit flips; s != 0 means r is random noise
s is the message that was encoded; it does not depend on errors
s is always length n and equals r when decoding succeeds
questions.explanation: The syndrome is the parity-check output. Zero syndrome means r lies in the code; nonzero indicates constraint violations (typically errors).

questions.question: Why is the brute-force decoder in this lesson not a realistic decoding method for cryptographic-size Goppa codes?
options: The number of error patterns grows combinatorially with n
The parity-check matrix stops being binary for large n
Field multiplication becomes undefined when m is large
Nullspace generators exist only when t is at least m
questions.explanation: Searching all weight-≤t error patterns costs roughly sum_{w≤t} C(n,w), which becomes astronomically large for real parameters.

questions.question: In McEliece/Niederreiter-style systems, what hard problem is the attacker believed to face given only a public, random-looking binary matrix?
options: Decoding a random linear code (syndrome decoding) without structure
Factoring the irreducible polynomial used to define GF(2^m)
Computing discrete logarithms in the multiplicative group of GF(2^m)
Finding a collision in a cryptographic hash function on demand
questions.explanation: Without the secret structure, decoding (or syndrome decoding) for general random-looking linear codes is believed computationally hard.
